source: Here's the stats for 600+ labels over the past 25 years:
why: This describes the scope of the dataset rather than a finding drawn from it, and the file contains 552 distinct Imprint values, so the '600+' count itself does not reproduce.

source: #8 in the ranking of labels by success on Billboard, Ruffhouse was a joint venture with Columbia, signing Fugees, Cypress Hill, Kris Kross, and Wyclef Jean.
why: Under the story's rank-and-weeks weighting (sum of 51 minus chart rank over all chart weeks), Ruffhouse ranks 11th, not 8th; the joint-venture and signing details are external roster information not present in the chart file.

source: In 1989, regional independent labels dominated with superstar signings: Young MC and the Pharcyde are signed to Delicious Vinyl. Biz Markie (Just a Friend), Big Daddy Kane (Smooth Operator), and Marley Marl are all on Cold Chillin’. Ruthless, Eazy E’s label, has N.W.A. and The D.O.C. on its roster. Jive is crushing it with a roster that includes Boogie Down Productions, DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince, and Too $hort. And Tommy Boy presciently released both De La Soul and Queen Latifah’s first albums.
why: The roster/signing statements and the independent-versus-major distinction cannot be checked from the chart file, which records no label ownership, signing dates or album releases. Jive's 1989 chart dominance is reproduced separately.

source: For the past 25 years, there’s always been mega-popular labels (e.g., Shady/Aftermath, Rawkus, No Limit, Bad Boy) – there were just more of them at one time.
why: The story gives no threshold for 'mega-popular', so the count of such labels depends on an arbitrary cutoff that the data cannot supply.

The table's per-label artist counts do not reproduce exactly: after removing feature credits from artist names the file gives Jive 41 instead of the story's 44 and Roc-A-Fella 17 instead of 18, although most rows match (e.g., Def Jam 48, Young Money 9, Bad Boy 29, Ruffhouse 14, Columbia 24).

source: Today, Young Money is dominating with a lineup of Nicki Minaj, Drake, Tyga, and Lil Wayne.
why: The lineup is roster information rather than a chart statistic; Young Money's chart dominance is reproduced in the yearly top-label fact.

source: XL Recordings (Adele, M.I.A., FKA Twigs) is one potential model, who keeps its roster small and typically releases no more than six albums a year.
why: Album-release counts and roster size are not in the chart file.

source: Rhymesayers’ model (who helped on this article) has sustained for 20 years, staying small and working with artists who have deep fan bases rather than the potential for massive commercial success.
why: Label longevity and business strategy are not chart statistics available in the file.

source: The top ten list reads like a history of hip hop.
why: Qualitative interpretation with no measurable claim.
